newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta increases 1996-97 budget surplus forecast.
newsitem.headline: Alberta increases 1996-97 budget surplus forecast.

text.p: The Canadian province of Alberta, buoyed by higher oil and gas prices, said on Tuesday it increased its 1996-97 budget surplus forecast to C$1.701 billion, C$1.377 billion higher than projected three months ago.
Alberta, in its second-quarter budget report, said the bigger surplus would result from higher revenues from non-renewable resources, personal and corporate taxes and lotteries.
The province said in August that the 1996-97 surplus was projected at C$325 million, but served notice that higher energy prices could push that up.
In the latest report, revenue was forecast at C$15.448 billion, C$1.764 billion above estimates made during the province's February budget.
Expenses for the fiscal year were projected at C$13.785 billion.
Under Alberta law, the entire surplus will be applied to its net debt, reducing it to C$4.522 billion at March 31, 1997. The amount excludes pension liabilities.
Due to the payment, Alberta's net debt was on track for elimination in 2006-07, it said.

Resource revenue was forecast at C$3.576 billion, a C$930 million increase from the budget forecast. The province said West Texas Intermediate oil prices were expected to average US$22 a barrel for the period, up from the budget forecast of C$18.50. Natural gas prices were expected to be unchanged from the previous forecast of C$1.45 per thousand cubic feet.

Strong land sale activity in the first half of the year was expected to add C$200 million to the budget amount, it said. A further C$246 million, set aside as a cushion against the possibility of weak energy prices, was now included in revenue, it said.
Alberta said interest cost savings from its lower debt would be spent on health care, where spending increased by C$145 million from the original budget.
